ta-l1d16q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for Distinctions 16–17, where Lombard descends to the special modes of the Spirit's mission: visible (Dist. 16) and invisible (Dist. 17). In Distinction 16 he distinguishes two modes of the Spirit's temporal procession and contrasts the Spirit's visible mission with the Son's. By his visible mission the Son is called less than the Father but not less than the Spirit. As man, however, the Son can be called less than the Father, the Spirit, and himself. Lombard also treats Hilary's claim that the Father is greater than the Son and yet the Son is not less. Four articles are announced: on visible mission in itself, to whom it should be made, in what forms, and by whose ministry.
claims: By the visible mission the Son as man is less than the Father, the Spirit, and himself, but not as God.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3522.summary: First objection against visible mission. Mission means a divine person being in something in a new way, but God cannot be in any visible creature in a new way. He is in all creatures by essence, power, and presence, and besides that in holy minds by grace, which cannot be in a bodily visible thing.
claims: God cannot be newly present in a visible bodily creature.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3525.summary: Anticipates the reply that God is in those visible creatures as in a sign. Every effect representing its cause is a sign by which one can reach the cause, and all creatures represent God as image or vestige, so he would be visibly sent in all creatures, not newly present in these.
claims: Every creature signifies God as image or vestige.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3528.summary: Second objection. The character of a sacrament is that God is in it as in a visible sign. If the Spirit is said to be visibly sent because he is in visible things as signs, those things would be sacraments, and there would be a visible mission in every sacrament.
claims: God is in a sacrament as in a visible sign.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3532.summary: Third objection. Augustine says the Spirit is visibly sent because some creaturely form was made in time in which he was visibly shown. But in the Old Testament apparitions divine persons were shown in visible creatures, as to Abraham (Gen. 18), so visible mission seems to be no different from apparition.
claims: Old Testament apparitions showed divine persons in visible forms.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3535.summary: Anticipates the reply that visible mission shows invisible mission, unlike apparition. Invisible mission makes someone worthy of God's love, but no one knows whether they are worthy of love or hatred (Eccles. 9:1), and it seems not useful to know, or it would not be hidden.
claims: No one knows whether they are worthy of love or hatred.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3541.summary: Fourth objection. Nothing manifests something unless it leads sufficiently to it, and no visible creature leads sufficiently to knowledge of invisible grace.
claims: No visible creature suffices to manifest invisible grace.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3544.summary: Thomas's determination. As the temporal procession is not essentially other than the eternal but adds a relation to a temporal effect, so the visible mission is not essentially other than the Spirit's invisible mission but adds only manifestation through a visible sign. Three things concur in the Spirit's visible mission: being sent by someone, being in another in a special way, and both being shown by a visible sign, by reason of which the whole mission is called visible.
claims: Visible mission is invisible mission plus manifestation through a visible sign.
It involves being sent, being specially present, and both being shown by a sign.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3547.summary: Reply to the first objection. The visible creature relates differently in the Son's and the Spirit's visible missions. In the Son's, it is not only that through which or in which mission is shown but that to which the mission is made, since he assumed a visible human nature into unity of person and is said to be visibly sent into flesh by that assumption. So he exists in a new way in the visible nature itself, by union in body as well as soul. In the Spirit's visible mission the visible creature is not that to which the mission is made but only shows an invisible mission made to someone, so the Spirit is newly in it only as in a sign and is newly in the person to whom the mission is made.
claims: In the Son's visible mission the visible nature is assumed and is the terminus of mission; in the Spirit's it is only a sign.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3550.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although every creature signifies God's being and goodness, none signifies his being in someone by grace unless specially instituted for this, as these visible creatures were specially made to indicate the Spirit's presence.
claims: Only specially instituted signs signify God's presence by grace.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3554.summary: Reply to the third argument. Sacraments signify the presence of divine indwelling as signs instituted not for a time but permanently, while these visible creatures were instituted to signify it only at a determinate time. Better: the sacraments of the Old Law signified future grace, not present grace, since they did not confer it, and the sacraments of the New Law are not only signs but in a way causes, so they signify grace not as already had but as to be produced through them. These forms, by contrast, are only signs of present grace and not causes; at Christ's baptism, to whom a visible mission was made, no invisible grace was produced in him. So all to whom visible missions were made had grace, whereas not all who receive sacraments receive grace, since the sacraments' causality can be impeded.
claims: Visible missions are signs of present grace, not causes; New Law sacraments are signs and causes of grace to be produced.
Old Law sacraments signified future grace without conferring it.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3557.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Visible mission includes apparition and adds the character of mission, which has two elements (origin and special indwelling). An apparition requires only that something divine be manifested in a visible sign, not that one person's origin from another or a special indwelling be manifested. At Mamre three appeared to show the number of persons, but the order by which one is from another was not shown. So apparition can belong to the Father, but visible mission cannot.
claims: Visible mission adds to apparition the manifestation of origin and indwelling.
The Father can appear but cannot be visibly sent.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3560.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. No one can know of themselves whether they are worthy of hatred or love, but it can be divinely revealed for some benefit, to them and to others too. What benefits one does not benefit all, so what is revealed to one need not be revealed to all.
claims: The state of grace can be divinely revealed to some for their benefit.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3563.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. Although a visible creature does not suffice to lead to knowledge of invisible mission, its novelty rouses observers to wonder and inquiry, and then those inquiring can be taught the invisible mission signified, through invisible grace and the preacher's external teaching.
claims: Visible signs prompt wonder and inquiry, completed by grace and preaching.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3575.summary: First argument that visible mission should have been made to the Old Testament fathers. Visible mission is a sign of invisible mission, and invisible missions were made to them (Dist. 15).
claims: The Old Testament fathers received invisible missions.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3578.summary: Second argument. New Testament grace is the grace of fullness, since we have all received from Christ's fullness. If the Spirit's mission was made to the early Church because of the fullness of grace, it should be made to all the faithful.
claims: All the faithful share in the fullness of grace.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3581.summary: Third argument. Through visible missions and signs the apostles spread the faith (Mark 16:20), and the prelates of our time are as bound to preach as they were, so visible missions should be made to them.
claims: Prelates are bound to preach as the apostles were.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3588.summary: Fourth argument. The Blessed Virgin had the fullest grace of all pure creatures. If visible mission shows the fullness of indwelling grace, a special visible mission should have been made to her.
claims: The Virgin had the fullest grace among pure creatures.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3591.summary: Contrary argument that no visible mission should have been made to Christ. Visible mission signifies invisible mission, and no invisible mission of the Spirit was made to Christ except perhaps at his conception, so none should have been made afterward.
claims: No invisible mission was made to Christ after his conception.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3594.summary: Thomas's determination. In invisible mission, grace overflows into the mind from the fullness of divine love, and through that effect the recipient receives experiential knowledge of the divine person. In visible mission there is a further degree of overflow: inner grace, by its fullness, overflows into a visible showing that manifests the person's indwelling not only to the recipient but to others. So two things are required: fullness of grace in the recipients, and that this fullness be ordered to others, so that abundant grace overflows into them. For this reason visible mission was made first to Christ and then to the apostles, through whom grace was spread to many, since through them the Church was planted.
claims: Visible mission signifies a fullness of grace that overflows to others.
It was made to Christ and the apostles, through whom grace spread and the Church was planted.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3597.summary: Reply to the first argument. Although some Old Testament fathers received the fullest personal grace, it was not yet the time of grace, because of the impediment of original sin, for which human nature had not yet received a remedy through Christ's death. So the fullness of grace was to be signified not as present but only as future, in apparitions and legal sacraments. Also it was not yet the time of spiritual propagation, by which various nations are spiritually reborn in the knowledge of God; divine worship passed from fathers to sons by carnal propagation. So grace was not to be signified by a visible mission, which signifies grace tending into others.
claims: Before Christ's death it was not the time of grace or of spiritual propagation, so no visible mission was made.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3600.summary: Reply to the second argument. The faithful of the early Church were a kind of spiritual seed through which faith was to sprout in all nations, so visible mission was made to them to show that through them the Church was to be planted in the knowledge of God throughout the world.
claims: The early Church received visible mission as the seed of the worldwide Church.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3603.summary: Reply to the third argument. Visible mission is not needed now as then for two reasons. First, the natural order is to come from visible to invisible things, so visible signs were shown to the first believers, still unformed in knowledge of God. Now that the faith is known and published, knowledge through invisible signs, the gifts of grace infused in minds, suffices, as a young plant needs support that is later removed. Second, those signs and visible missions were a kind of argument confirming the truth of the faith, and once a proof is complete it need not be repeated; one proceeds on the supposition of the earlier proof.
claims: Visible missions are no longer needed: the faith, once established, proceeds from invisible signs and from the earlier, completed proof.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3607.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. A visible mission of the Spirit was made to the Blessed Virgin at Pentecost among the others of the early Church. But although she attained a singular fullness of grace, no special visible mission was made to her, since her grace was not ordered to planting the Church by teaching and administering sacraments as the apostles' was. Hence 'I do not permit a woman to speak in the church' (1 Tim. 2:12).
claims: The Virgin received the visible mission at Pentecost but no special one, since her grace was not ordered to teaching and sacramental ministry.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3613.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. A visible mission need not show an invisible mission made at that time; it suffices that one was made earlier. Why a visible mission was then made to Christ is explained in the next article.
claims: A visible mission may signify an earlier invisible one.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3625.summary: First argument that visible mission is not only in bodily form. There are three kinds of vision, bodily, imaginary, and intellectual (Isidore's Gloss), and divine things can be manifested by each. As there is a mission by intellectual vision (invisible grace) and by bodily vision (bodily forms), so there should be one by imaginary vision.
claims: Divine things can be manifested in bodily, imaginary, and intellectual vision.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3628.summary: Second argument. The nobler a thing, the nobler its properties, and a nobler creature represents divine goodness by nobler properties. So visible mission, which manifests the divine persons, should always be through the noblest creatures, such as a star, not a dove or fire.
claims: Nobler creatures represent God better.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3631.summary: Third argument. No pretence befits the Spirit of truth (John 15), so he should not appear in forms with no reality beneath them. The dove would then be a true animal and the tongues of fire true tongues and fire, which seems false, since the fire did not burn and the dove returned to its prior matter after its office, as the saints say. Also, if they were true things, they would not lead to something else.
claims: The Spirit of truth cannot appear in false forms.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3635.summary: Fourth argument. The Spirit is one ('we have all drunk of one Spirit', 1 Cor. 12:13), and a sign should correspond to what it signifies, so he should have appeared in only one sign.
claims: A sign should correspond to the one it signifies.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3641.summary: Fifth argument. As the Spirit is sent invisibly into the mind, so is the Son, and both missions order someone to planting the Church. So as the Spirit was sent visibly to some, the Son should be too, apart from his assuming flesh.
claims: The Son's invisible mission also orders one to planting the Church.
concepts: visible mission of the Son without incarnation

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3644.summary: Thomas's determination. Visible mission signifies a fullness of grace overflowing into many, which is why it is manifested to others. Grace overflows in two ways: by instruction and by operation, insofar as the one with fullness of grace is in some way an efficient cause of grace. Both were in Christ. He led us to knowledge of God by his teaching (John 1:18), and he gave grace effectively as God and by way of merit as man. To signify the overflow of his grace into us by operation, the visible mission was made to him at his baptism, when, receiving nothing from baptism, he gave regenerating life to the waters by the touch of his most pure flesh, effectively as God and meritoriously as man. So the Spirit came on him in the form of a dove, the most fecund animal, to signify spiritual fecundity, and the Father spoke attesting his natural sonship, in whose likeness we are reborn as adopted sons by baptismal grace (Rom. 8:29). To signify the overflow of grace from him into others by teaching, the Spirit appeared over him in a bright cloud at the transfiguration, a cloud whose nature is to spread light (Job 37:11), signifying the spreading of teaching through preaching (Gregory), and the Father's voice added 'hear him'. So the visible mission to Christ was not needed from his conception but when his grace began to overflow into others. Likewise a visible mission was made twice to the apostles: first, to signify their overflow of grace by operation, in administering sacraments, in the form of breath (John 20:22–23, 'whose sins you forgive'). This showed that such authority came to them only from the influx of the head, Christ, whereas to Christ it came immediately from the Father, signified by the dove descending from above, in the apostles by breath proceeding from Christ. Second, to signify their overflow by teaching, at Pentecost (Acts 2), in tongues of fire, so that they would be fluent in words and fervent in charity, zealous for their neighbours' salvation.
claims: Visible missions signify grace overflowing by operation (sacramental) or by instruction (teaching).
To Christ: the dove at the baptism (operation) and the bright cloud at the transfiguration (teaching).
To the apostles: breath (sacramental authority from Christ the head) and tongues of fire at Pentecost (teaching).

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3672.summary: Reply to the first argument. Imaginary vision is properly called revelation, not apparition or mission, and such visions were often given to the prophets. Visible mission shows the presence of indwelling grace, and a species in the imagination is not necessarily of something present, as a species in sense is. So inner mission is better manifested by bodily forms seen externally than by imaginary ones.
claims: Imaginary visions are revelations, not missions, since they do not show something present.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3675.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although nobler creatures more expressly resemble divine perfection as to the essential attributes, as to one person's going out from another and the mode of the gifts' procession from God and their effects, a more fitting likeness can be found in humbler creatures, such as fecundity in the dove and speech in the tongue, which visible mission had to signify. Alternatively, following Dionysius, lower creatures, being further from participating the divine persons, manifest divine things more fittingly, since their evident distance prevents error; it would be easy to err by believing some divinity is in a star or another noble creature.
claims: Humble creatures can better signify the persons' processions and gifts, and avoid idolatry.
Dionysius: lowly signs prevent the error of attributing divinity to them.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3678.summary: Reply to the third argument. The dove was not a true, natural animal but a likeness of a dove visibly shown in matter prepared for this, which returned to its prior matter after its office. There was no pretence, since the likeness was shown not to manifest any truth about a dove but to manifest the properties of the invisible mission. So the sign was not false: what was signified corresponded to the sign and the thing to the likeness, as one speaking metaphorically does not lie, intending not the things the words name but those they resemble. The same holds of the fire. But the visible nature in which the Son appeared was assumed into being and not only as a sign, so it had to have true human being.
claims: The dove and fire were true signs but not true animals or fire, like metaphors.
The Son's visible nature, being assumed, had to be truly human.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3682.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The forms in which the Spirit appeared signify his effects, according to which the Spirit is called manifold though substantially one (Wis. 7:22), so he appeared in several forms and several times. Because the visible nature in which the Son appeared was assumed into one being in the person of God's Son, there is only one such mission, as there is one personal being.
claims: The Spirit's many forms signify his many effects; the Son has one visible mission, as one personal being.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3685.summary: Reply to the last argument. Appearing in another's form, included in visible mission, fits only what has no form of its own in which to be seen bodily. Visible mission was not to be before the time of grace, which began when the Son of God assumed flesh. Since he assumed it inseparably, whenever a visible mission is fitting he always has his own visible form in which he can be seen. So the only visible mission that fits him is the one in the assumed nature. Why the Spirit did not assume a nature into unity of person is asked in Book III.
claims: The Son, having his own visible form since the incarnation, has no visible mission other than the incarnation.
concepts: one visible mission of the Son

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3698.summary: First argument that the visible forms were not formed by angels' ministry. Augustine says God's words in the New Testament were made not through angels but by God himself, so the voice 'This is my beloved Son' (Matt. 17:5) was not formed by angels, nor the other things pertaining to visible mission.
claims: New Testament divine speech was made by God himself.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3704.summary: Second argument. An angel is united to a body it forms as mover to moved. If angels formed these forms, they would be bodies assumed by angels, and an angel, not a divine person, would be said to be sent in them.
claims: Bodies formed by angels are assumed by angels.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3707.summary: Third argument. As the Son's visible mission was by his assumed body, the Spirit's was by these forms, and angels in no way formed Christ's assumed body, so they did not form these forms either.
claims: Angels did not form Christ's body.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3711.summary: Sed contra from Gregory on the voice answering the Son ('I have glorified it and will glorify it', John 12:28): speaking of heavenly things, God formed his words, which he wished humans to hear, through the ministry of a rational creature. The same holds for the others.
claims: Gregory: God formed audible words through a rational creature's ministry.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3720.summary: Second sed contra. According to Dionysius, the law of divinity is that the last are perfected by the first through the middle, and angels are between God and bodily creatures, so operations on bodily creatures are done through angels.
claims: The last are perfected by the first through intermediaries.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3723.summary: Thomas's determination. There are two opinions. Some say Old Testament apparitions were made through angels while New Testament missions were made immediately by the divine persons, which is why the persons and not angels are said to be sent in these forms. Others say both were by angels' ministry. Each is true in part. In both there is an outer appearance and something inwardly effected or signified, but differently. In Old Testament apparitions the outer appearance does not refer as sign to what is inward but to something else, such as the Trinity, and the inward element is only the soul's knowledge or illumination about what the signs signify. Since divine illuminations come to us through angels (Dionysius), both outer and inner were done by angels' ministry there, and so there was no mission of a divine person, which concerns only the person's immediate effect. In visible mission, the outer appearance is a sign of what was done inwardly, then or before, and the inward element is not only knowledge but an effect of sanctifying grace, immediately from the divine person, by reason of which the person is said to be sent. So in visible mission the inward element was produced immediately without angels, while angels ministered to the outward element, as Gregory says.
claims: In visible missions the inner effect of grace is immediately from the divine person, while angels minister the outward signs.
In Old Testament apparitions both outer sign and inner illumination were by angels, so there was no mission.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3726.summary: Reply to the first argument. Augustine speaks of the words the Son of God uttered in his assumed body, which were plainly uttered immediately by God.
claims: Augustine refers to Christ's own speech.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3729.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although an angel acts on the outwardly appearing creature, it does not act on the inner effect, by reason of which the divine person is said to be sent. Nor is it unfitting that a divine person and an angel be sent together.
claims: A divine person and an angel can be sent together in different respects.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3732.summary: Reply to the third argument. The assumed body is united to the divine person in one personal being, so it was not fitting, given its dignity, that it be formed other than by God. The same reasoning does not hold for the others.
claims: Christ's body, united in personal being, was fittingly formed by God alone.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3736.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Gregory's statement applies only to the outward element, not to what is inwardly signified.
claims: Angelic ministry concerns only the outward sign.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3739.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Dionysius's law holds for effects that can come from a creature, and grace is not such an effect. So angels act on the outward element of visible mission, not on the inward one.
claims: Grace cannot be produced by creatures, so angels do not mediate it.

ta-l1d16q1-d1e3748.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'Made a little lower than the angels' seems to conflict with the Gloss on Hebrews that the human nature assumed by the Son is better than everything but God. The Son is lower in a qualified sense, through bodily suffering, not because the assumed nature is inferior in that individual, though it is not true universally that human nature is not inferior to angels. (2) On Hilary's claim that the Father is greater and the Son not lesser, which seems impossible since greater and lesser are correlative: some say the Father is greater because he has more notions, while the Son is not lesser because innascibility has no corresponding notion in him. Thomas rejects this, since equality is not measured by relations (Dist. 19), more properties do not make anything greater, and it is contrary to Hilary's intent. Instead, giver and receiver can be compared as to what is given or as to the character of giving. As to what is given, a giver is sometimes greater (when the receiver receives less) and sometimes equal (as in univocal generation), never less. As to the character of giving, the giver has a dignity from giving, while the receiver has no imperfection from receiving unless it receives imperfectly. So as to what is given, the Father is not greater nor the Son lesser. As to the character of giving, the giver's dignity is not taken from the Father, and by reason of it he is called greater, 'greater' implying perfection of dignity rather than comparison of magnitude. Since the Son receives perfectly all the Father has, no lessening fits him. Though the saints attribute authority to the Father, they do not attribute 'sub-authority' to the Son; that is an abuse of language. (3) 'The image of innascibility' means the Father gives the Son being as image of his unbegotten self by a sacred and secret birth.
claims: The incarnate Son is 'lower than the angels' only in his passible body.
The Father is 'greater' by the dignity of giving, while the Son, receiving perfectly, is not lesser.
Authority is attributed to the Father, but no 'sub-authority' to the Son.

ta-l1d16q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 16 places the visible mission of the Spirit among the special modes of mission. It notes Lombard's comparison with the Son's visible mission, by which the Son is less as man, and Hilary's 'greater without lesser', and announces four articles on visible mission.

ta-l1d16q1-Dd1e3514.summary: Article 1 asks whether visible mission belongs to a divine person. Thomas holds that visible mission is the invisible mission plus manifestation by a visible sign. In the Son's mission the visible nature is assumed and is itself the terminus. In the Spirit's mission the visible creature is only a specially instituted sign of an invisible mission to someone. These forms signify present grace without causing it, unlike New Law sacraments, which signify and cause grace to come. Visible mission adds to apparition the manifestation of origin and indwelling, so the Father can appear but not be sent. The state of grace can be revealed to some for their benefit, and visible signs prompt inquiry completed by grace and preaching.
claims: Visible mission is invisible mission manifested by a visible sign.
The Son's visible mission is the incarnation; the Spirit's visible forms are only signs.

ta-l1d16q1-Dd1e3567.summary: Article 2 asks to whom visible mission should be made. Thomas holds that it signifies a fullness of grace overflowing into others, so it was made to Christ and the apostles, through whom the Church was planted. It was not made to the Old Testament fathers, since it was not yet the time of grace or of spiritual propagation. It is no longer needed, since the faith now proceeds from invisible signs and from its once-completed proof. The Virgin received it with the others at Pentecost but not specially, since her grace was not ordered to teaching and sacramental ministry.
claims: Visible mission is made to those whose fullness of grace overflows to others: Christ and the apostles.

ta-l1d16q1-Dd1e3617.summary: Article 3 asks in what forms visible mission is made. Grace overflows by operation and by instruction. To Christ the Spirit came as a dove at the baptism, signifying his life-giving operation and spiritual fecundity, and as a bright cloud at the transfiguration, signifying teaching. To the apostles he came as Christ's breath, signifying sacramental authority from the head, and as tongues of fire at Pentecost, signifying teaching. The forms were bodily rather than imaginary and lowly rather than noble, to signify the processions and avoid idolatry. They were true signs like metaphors, not true animals, and several in number for the Spirit's many effects, while the Son's one visible mission is the incarnation.
claims: The Spirit's visible forms signify overflow of grace by operation (dove, breath) or by teaching (cloud, tongues of fire).
The Son's only visible mission is the incarnation.
concepts: dove, cloud, breath, tongues of fire

ta-l1d16q1-Dd1e3690.summary: Article 4 asks whether the visible forms were formed by angels. Thomas takes a middle position. In visible missions the inner effect, sanctifying grace, is immediately from the divine person, while angels minister the outward signs. In Old Testament apparitions both the outward sign and the inward illumination were angelic, so there was no mission. Dionysius's law of mediation does not extend to grace, which no creature can produce.
claims: Angels form the outward signs of visible missions, but grace is produced by the divine person immediately.

ta-l1d16q1-Dd1e3743.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 16 explains that the incarnate Son is lower than the angels only through bodily suffering. It interprets Hilary's 'the Father is greater yet the Son not lesser' through the dignity of the giver and the perfection of the Son's reception, rejecting any 'sub-authority' of the Son.
claims: The Father is greater by the dignity of giving; the Son, receiving perfectly, is not lesser.

ta-l1d16q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 16 treats the visible mission of the Holy Spirit. Article 1 holds that visible mission is invisible mission manifested by a visible sign. The Son's visible mission is the incarnation, in which the visible nature is assumed, while the Spirit's visible forms are only instituted signs of present grace, unlike New Law sacraments, which also cause grace. Article 2 holds that visible mission signifies a fullness of grace overflowing to others, so it was made to Christ and the apostles as founders of the Church. It was not made to the Old Testament fathers, before the time of grace, and it is no longer needed now that the faith is established. Article 3 interprets the forms: the dove and breath signify overflow of grace by operation, sacramental and life-giving, and the bright cloud and tongues of fire signify overflow by teaching. Article 4 holds that angels minister the outward signs, while the inner grace is immediately from the divine person. The Expositio interprets Hilary on the Father as 'greater' without the Son being lesser.
claims: Visible mission is the manifestation of invisible mission through a sign of overflowing grace.
Visible missions were made to Christ and the apostles to signify grace overflowing by operation and teaching for the Church.
Angels form the outward signs, but grace is from the divine person immediately.
concepts: dove, cloud, breath, tongues of fire
